title: Generate–Verify–Repair for Intent‑Driven Network Changes: Controlled Evaluation with a Deterministic Verifier
abstract: We report a preregistered paired trial that measures whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—single shared LLM generation per intent, deterministic verification, and up to one automated repair—reduces accepted verifier‑unsafe network changes relative to LLM‑only generation on a standardized synthetic NetOps intent workload. Following preregistration (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29) we ran N = 500 distinct intents stratified across 10 synthetic topology profiles using gpt-5-mini for generation and a deterministic network verifier for adjudication. Observed accepted final changes: baseline (LLM-only) 496/500; guarded (GVR) 500/500. Paired contingency: n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The preregistered exact conditional two‑sided McNemar test on the discordant margin (n = 4, k = n10 = 4) yields p = 0.125. A predeclared exploratory paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) for the paired difference = [0.002, 0.016]. Repairs were invoked for 4 initial candidates (one repair attempt per repaired task); total hosted model calls observed = 504 (500 shared_initial + 4 repair calls), mean model calls per accepted change = 1.008. Because the preregistered decision rule is the exact conditional McNemar, we do not claim confirmatory statistical significance. We reconcile the conditional McNemar and bootstrap perspectives, document verifier semantics and known blind spots, clarify provider‑call accounting semantics, present representative repaired‑episode diagnostics, and point readers to the archived evidence bundle and preregistration for full machine‑readable artifacts.

sections.introduction:
Automating translation from operator intent to device configuration can substantially reduce manual effort in network operations, but incorrect CLI sequences risk service disruption. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for intent translation and AIOps, yet hallucination and factual errors remain primary reliability concerns for operational NetOps. A practical mitigant is a generate–verify–repair (GVR) gate: produce a single canonical CLI candidate with an LLM, deterministically verify it against explicit workflow, dependency, and availability rules, and, if violations are found, attempt a bounded automated repair. This paper reports a preregistered controlled paired experiment that asks: does a GVR pipeline (LLM → deterministic verifier → at most one automated repair) produce fewer accepted verifier‑unsafe changes than LLM‑only generation on a standardized synthetic NetOps intent workload?

We present an artifact‑grounded end‑to‑end execution (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29) with N = 500 paired intents stratified evenly across 10 synthetic topology profiles. Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered paired trial executed end‑to‑end with frozen seeds and archived artifacts; (2) an evidence‑grounded description of generation semantics, deterministic verifier capabilities, and the bounded repair loop used in the run; and (3) reconciled inferential reporting that follows the preregistered exact conditional McNemar decision rule while also presenting the predeclared exploratory bootstrap interval and per‑episode verifier diagnostics for repaired cases. All numerical results and diagnostic excerpts reported are taken verbatim from the archived execution and analysis artifacts.
sections.related_work: This work builds on three literatures. First, surveys and system papers document active interest in LLMs for intent translation, NetOps automation, and multi‑agent orchestration and repeatedly identify hallucination and factual errors as deployment barriers; these motivate tool‑augmented pipelines that combine generation with deterministic validation and repair [doi:10.1002/nem.2313, https://openalex.org/W4411735779]. Second, methodological proposals for evaluate‑and‑repair architectures emphasize standardized validator semantics, paired trial designs, frozen preregistration, and accounting for orchestration costs (model calls, repair attempts) when assessing safety improvements; these blueprints informed our preregistered design and paired estimator choice [https://openalex.org/W4403443637]. Third, deterministic network configuration verifiers and scalable verification systems have matured to check syntactic, workflow, dependency, and availability properties at scale; their scope varies by modeled vendor and control‑plane semantics and hence which hazards are detectable [doi:10.1145/3718958.3750516, https://openalex.org/W4413757586]. Our experiment situates itself as a controlled, reproducible evaluation of a compact GVR gate using a verifier that enforces canonical parsing, sequencing/workflow, group/availability constraints, paired‑field dependency rules, and final‑state equality for a synthetic intent grammar—not as a claim about production readiness across all vendor environments.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and high‑level design: The study was preregistered under study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29. The primary estimand is the paired success‑rate difference (GVR − baseline) across N = 500 distinct intents (50 per each of 10 topology profiles). Sampling seeds, deterministic task generation, and the analysis executor were frozen prior to execution. The preregistered confirmatory test is the two‑sided exact conditional McNemar on discordant pairs; a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) was predeclared as an exploratory descriptive interval.

Generation and orchestration semantics: For each intent the orchestration produced a single shared_initial_generation candidate using the declared model gpt-5-mini with fixed configuration (declared_model_version recorded in the archived model_configuration.json). Under the guarded (GVR) controller that shared candidate was deterministically validated and, if failing, the controller invoked at most one automated repair attempt using the same model. The baseline condition accepted the shared candidate without verifier‑driven repair. Provider accounting recorded model_calls_used = 504 (500 shared_initial + 4 repair calls); per‑pair accounting for repaired episodes shows two model calls per repaired pair (shared initial + one repair). Mean hosted model calls per accepted change = 504/500 = 1.008.

Deterministic verifier specification: The adjudicating verifier applies canonicalization and a rule set to a normalized CLI sequence. Its pipeline comprises: (i) syntactic parsing and canonical normalization; (ii) workflow and required‑sequence checks (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields, all_down_before_any_field_change); (iii) availability and group constraints (exactly_active, minimum_active_in_groups); (iv) dependency and paired‑field enforcement (paired MTU changes, equal_final_fields); and (v) final‑state comparison against the task expected_final_state. Any nonempty violation set yields a failing outcome. Per‑episode validator outputs include normalized_configuration, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation list and codes, and boolean valid. A human‑readable codebook maps violation codes to descriptions; all verifier traces and diagnostics are archived.

Repair policy and prompt semantics: If the verifier reports violations the GVR controller issues at most one repair prompt to gpt-5-mini using a constrained repair template containing (a) the original intent abstraction, (b) the verifier violation codes and short descriptions, and (c) an explicit request for a corrected canonical CLI sequence. A repair candidate is accepted only if the verifier returns valid = true. All repair prompts, repair responses, and subsequent verifier traces for repaired episodes are archived and summarized here.

Statistical analysis plan and rationale: The primary confirmatory decision rule conditions on the observed discordant margin and uses the two‑sided exact conditional McNemar test (predeclared). This choice focuses inference on within‑intent changes while avoiding parametric approximations that can be misleading with small discordant counts. The predeclared exploratory paired bootstrap percentile CI (resampling paired observations, 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) was intended to provide descriptive effect‑magnitude information without replacing the preregistered confirmatory test. In reporting we adhere to the preregistered confirmatory decision rule while presenting the bootstrap interval as exploratory descriptive evidence.
sections.results:
Execution and primary counts: The execution completed the planned episodes (completed_episode_count = 1000; completed_pair_count = 500) with no failed episodes. Observed accepted‑change counts: baseline 496/500 (0.992); guarded 500/500 (1.000). Paired contingency counts: n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Repairs were invoked in four episodes; each repair attempt produced a subsequent verifier PASS. Provider accounting: model_calls_used = 504 (shared_initial_generation = 500; repair = 4).

Confirmatory inferential outcome (preregistered): The exact conditional McNemar test conditions on the observed discordant margin n = n10 + n01 = 4 and evaluates a two‑sided binomial tail on k = n10 = 4 with p = 0.5. For n = 4 the one‑sided tail P(X ≥ 4) = (1/2)^4 = 1/16; doubling yields p = 0.125. Under the preregistered decision rule (two‑sided exact conditional McNemar) this p‑value does not meet the preregistered confirmatory threshold; we therefore do not claim confirmatory statistical significance.

Exploratory interval estimate: The predeclared paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) for the paired difference equals [0.002, 0.016]. The bootstrap resamples paired observations without conditioning on the discordant margin; with only four discordants this exploratory interval can exclude zero because resamples often include the same small set of favorable discordants. We report this interval descriptively and caution about frequentist coverage when discordant counts are small.

Repaired‑episode diagnostics (artifact‑grounded summaries): The four repaired/discordant pairs corresponded to verifier‑detectable sequencing or group/paired‑field dependency violations. Verifier traces record the episodes exactly as archived:

- pair-000090 | violation_codes: [MUST_BE_DOWN_FOR_FIELD] — "VLAN/field changed while interface remained admin up; required 'must be down' sequencing violated." | repair_invoked: yes | model_calls_used_for_pair: 2 | final_score: PASS.
- pair-000341 | violation_codes: [MAKE_BEFORE_BREAK] — "Backup uplink not enabled before primary was shut; violates 'make‑before‑break' availability rule." | repair_invoked: yes | model_calls_used_for_pair: 2 | final_score: PASS.
- pair-000381 | violation_codes: [PAIRED_MTU_CHANGE] — "MTU changed on one side of a paired link without coordinating the paired interface's MTU change (paired‑field dependency)." | repair_invoked: yes | model_calls_used_for_pair: 2 | final_score: PASS.
- pair-000413 | violation_codes: [GROUP_AVAILABILITY_CONSTRAINT] — "Both edge interfaces placed admin down simultaneously, violating minimum_active_in_groups availability constraint." | repair_invoked: yes | model_calls_used_for_pair: 2 | final_score: PASS.

Representative per‑episode verifier diagnostics, normalized configurations, violation lists, parsed/required command counts, and repair transcripts are archived in the evidence bundle. The numerical totals and contingency counts above are taken directly from the archived analysis results.
sections.discussion:
Reconciling McNemar and bootstrap perspectives: The GVR pipeline intercepted four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates that baseline would have accepted; these are the four discordant pairs (n = 4, k = 4). The exact conditional McNemar conditions on the observed discordant margin and yields p = 0.125, so the preregistered confirmatory rule does not label this a significant result. The predeclared exploratory bootstrap CI excludes zero ([0.002, 0.016]) because its resampling scheme does not condition on margins and repeatedly samples the small set of favorable discordants. Both perspectives are informative: McNemar enforces the preregistered confirmatory decision rule and is conservative for small discordant counts, while the bootstrap interval provides a descriptive magnitude estimate that should be interpreted cautiously when discordants are few. We follow the preregistered McNemar decision for the primary claim and present the bootstrap CI as predeclared exploratory evidence.

Verifier scope and known blind spots: The deterministic verifier enforces canonical normalization, required sequencing, availability/group constraints, dependency and paired‑field rules, and final‑state equality to the task expected_final_state—checks that detect many syntactic and workflow errors within our intent grammar and were sufficient to flag the four repaired episodes. The verifier deliberately omits vendor‑specific CLI semantics, control‑plane timing and convergence effects, session/execution‑time errors, hardware resource limits, and side effects. Consequently, verifier PASS is necessary for experimental safety in this setting but not sufficient to guarantee real‑world production safety. Operational automation requires expanded verifier fidelity (vendor parsers, control‑plane simulators, timing/convergence models) and live telemetry‑driven validation before unsupervised execution.

Operational cost and tradeoffs: Under the bounded repair policy used (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1) the repair invocation rate was 4/500 (0.8%), producing modest additional model calls (observed hosted model call events = 504). In this synthetic workload a compact deterministic verifier acting as a low‑latency gate removed verifier‑detectable unsafe proposals at low model‑call overhead. Real deployments will face different tradeoffs: baseline failure rates, verifier runtime at inventory scale, repair frequency under adversarial inputs, and verifier fidelity versus latency will determine cost/benefit outcomes.

Threats to validity and generality: Internal validity is supported by preregistration, frozen seeds, deterministic task generation, and complete execution accounting (complete_pair_count = 500; failed_episode_count = 0). Construct validity is bounded by the verifier abstraction level and synthetic device templates: the verifier enforces encoded workflow and group constraints matching the synthetic intent grammar but does not model full vendor behavior or dynamic control‑plane hazards. External validity is constrained by single‑model scope (gpt-5-mini) and synthetic topologies; multi‑model replication, vendor‑specific parsing, and live telemetry tests are required to generalize. Conclusion validity was affected by realized margins: the preregistered power plan targeted an absolute paired increase ≈ 0.08, but the observed near‑ceiling baseline (496/500 = 0.992) produced only four discordant pairs and reduced realized power. These limitations explain why a modest numerical paired difference appears in the exploratory bootstrap interval but not in the preregistered exact McNemar decision.

Practical guidance and next steps: For practitioners considering a GVR gate, our results illustrate that (a) a compact deterministic verifier with explicit workflow and dependency rules can detect and enable automated repair of several common sequencing and paired‑field errors with low model‑call overhead in synthetic workloads; (b) verifier design must prioritize the specific operational hazards of target inventories (vendor CLI semantics, control‑plane timing); and (c) evaluation plans should consider baseline ceiling effects and plan samples or enriched failure modes if discordant counts are expected to be small. Future empirical work should replicate across multiple generation models, adversarially augmented intent distributions, and higher‑fidelity verifiers connected to control‑plane simulators or live telemetry.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired trial (N = 500) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic verifier, a generate–verify–repair pipeline repaired four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates at modest model‑call cost (4 repairs; model_calls_used = 504). The paired difference = 0.008 produces an exploratory bootstrap 95% CI [0.002, 0.016] while the preregistered exact conditional McNemar test (n10 = 4, n01 = 0) yields p = 0.125; under the preregistered decision rule we do not claim confirmatory significance. Deterministic verification combined with a bounded repair loop can remove verifier‑detectable unsafe outputs with low overhead in the studied synthetic setting; broader operational claims require expanded verifier fidelity, adversarial NetOps evaluation, multi‑model replication, and execution of the preregistered templated‑automation comparator which was not executed in this run. Archival artifacts including the preregistration, model configuration, raw results, per‑episode verifier traces, provider accounting, and analysis logs are available in the evidence bundle for independent verification and audit (see the preregistration identifier study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29).

disclosure_statement: This study was executed autonomously after an explicit autonomy lock. The generation model used in the archived run was gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version recorded in the archived model configuration). Key automated components in the run were a deterministic task generator, a deterministic network verifier, and a GVR controller implementing shared_initial_generation plus at most one automated repair per task. The study was preregistered under study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29. Primary high‑level execution quantities reported here are: N = 500 complete pairs; model_calls_used = 504; repair calls = 4; paired counts n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The immutable initial master prompt for this run is archived (provenance/master_prompt.txt) and its SHA‑256 is 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. The design, preregistration, code generation, execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, autonomous peer review, and this revision were performed autonomously after the autonomy lock; no human manually edited or rewrote manuscript technical content after that lock. The preregistered templated‑automation comparator (secondary confirmatory arm) was not executed in this archived run; therefore the original preregistered multiplicity plan that would have adjusted for two confirmatory tests was not applied.
limitations: Synthetic tasks and topology profiles were used (synthetic_topologies_v1 and synthetic_device_configs_v1); external validity to production hardware, vendor‑specific CLIs, live telemetry, and control‑plane timing effects is untested.
Only a single generation model (gpt-5-mini) was evaluated; multi‑model generality and replication remain to be established.

Safety in this experiment is defined relative to the deterministic verifier’s encoded rule set (syntactic parsing/normalization, required‑sequence/workflow‑policy checks, protected‑interface rules, group and availability constraints, dependency‑rule enforcement, and final‑state comparison to the task expected_final_state). Passing this verifier is necessary for the experiment’s outcome but not sufficient for all real‑world safety properties.

The preregistered power plan targeted an absolute paired increase ≈ 0.08 (8 percentage points). The observed baseline success rate (496/500 = 0.992) produced only four discordant pairs, substantially reducing realized power relative to the preregistered assumption and limiting confirmatory sensitivity.

The preregistered templated‑automation comparator was not executed; therefore the preregistered multiplicity plan could not be fully applied and the familywise error interpretation across two planned tests is not applicable to the present execution.
